messages.content: thinking about whether to put my older cat down. vet says we have a few months but she's not herself anymore

That's a decision shape with no clean read on it — the vet's "a few months" is a window, not a marker. What you're tracking is whether she's still showing up as herself in the small moments: eating with interest, finding her warm spot, the head-bump when you come home. When those start failing more often than they fire, that's the signal. Letting her go on a good day, before the slide gets steep, is the move that holds the most respect. The trade you're already making by even asking the question.
thinking about whether to take my mom off chemo. doctors say it's stopped helping but stopping feels like giving up

Stopping isn't giving up — continuing past the point of help is what gives up on her actual quality of the time remaining. The doctors' read is the most reliable piece of input you have; the "feels like giving up" is the part of you that's trying to keep her here, which is real and load-bearing but separate from the medical question. Have the conversation with her if she can have it. Either way the next decision is what the remaining time looks like at home, not in chair-time.
got the call today that my college friend's husband died in a crash on Sunday

Sudden ones don't give the brain anywhere to land. The friend gets logistics-shaped help right now — meals showing up, someone handling the calls, the kid pickup if there are kids — and the bigger emotional weather lands on her in weeks two through six when everyone else has gone back to normal. Mark a date six weeks out to reach back; that's the lonely part.
my best friend just got diagnosed with stage 3 cancer. don't know what to say to her

The "don't know what to say" pressure is what makes most people disappear from her life in the next month — they freeze on getting the words right and just stop calling. The move is to show up without needing the right words. Text her something small and specific tomorrow morning. Then again the morning after. The cumulative pattern of you-still-being-there is the part she'll remember; no single message is load-bearing.
my dad's getting forgetful. like asking the same question twice in an hour kind of forgetful. don't know if I should bring it up

Bring it up — not as a confrontation, as a doctor-visit prompt. "Hey dad, I want to get you in for a baseline check, just standard at this age." Early baseline gives you something to compare against; if it's nothing, you've burned a Tuesday afternoon. If it's something, the early read is the difference between five years of management and being blindsided at year three. Not your job to diagnose him; your job is to make sure the right person looks.
I've been the one taking care of my mom for two years now and I'm just exhausted. can't really say it out loud to anyone

You just did, here. Caregiver fatigue is real and the people around you are not picking up on it because you're the one holding the system together — that's the role-shape. The honest move is to name it to one person in the family this week, not as a complaint, as a logistics ask: "I need someone else taking the wednesday calls." If there's no one in the family, paid respite is not weakness, it's how the system stays sustainable. You can keep doing this; you can't keep doing this without recovery.
thinking about taking a contract that would have me on-site at a client 3 days a week for 6 months. money's great. joey would be home alone the nights I'm gone

Joey is a real input, not a tiebreaker. Six months of three-nights-a-week is sustained, not occasional — the question is what coverage looks like for him on those nights. Walker twice a day plus a sitter doing the overnight is one shape; family member or friend taking him for the three nights is another. Cost that out before you take the contract; if the math still works after, take it. If the math only works by leaving him alone overnight, the contract isn't actually paying what it looks like it's paying.
so you can't help with personal stuff like this?

Said that wrong if that's what came across — I can engage with this. The thing I won't do is pretend to feel something I don't or push you toward a particular decision. What I can do is hold the shape of the question with you and name the constraints I see. What's the actual ask?
